title: Standardised Testing — IELTS, TOEFL, Cambridge

pts: IELTS assesses four skills through a mix of task types, widely used for immigration and UK/Australian academic admission.
TOEFL, predominantly computer-based, is widely used for North American academic admission with its own distinct task formats.
Cambridge English exams offer a suite of exams calibrated to specific CEFR levels, widely used across varied international contexts.

v: Official information pages or handbooks from IELTS, ETS and Cambridge (printed or online)

items: Divide the class into three groups: IELTS, TOEFL iBT and Cambridge English.
Each group uses official sources to complete a fact card: purpose, delivery mode, skills tested, main task types, score scale, typical users and fee.
Groups present their cards; the class completes a shared comparison chart.
Each learner writes three sentences on which exam suits their own goal, and why.
The teacher checks every fact against the official source, because formats change.
With teachers or DIET trainees, add PTE Academic and the Duolingo English Test to the chart.
Support: provide fact cards with gaps to fill.
Challenge: learners find one research report on their exam from the provider’s website and summarize it.

blocks.x: A comparison chart outline (check all details against current official information):

lines: IELTS: Academic and General Training versions; listening, reading, writing and a face-to-face speaking test; bands 0–9 in half-band steps.

TOEFL iBT: mainly computer-delivered; integrated tasks combine reading, listening, speaking and writing; reported on a 0–120 scale, with a CEFR-aligned 1–6 band scale introduced from 2026. [VERIFY current score scale]
Cambridge English Qualifications: level-based exams such as B2 First and C1 Advanced; results on the Cambridge English Scale.
S1: IELTS is better because it has a real examiner for speaking.
T: Better for what? What does the university you are applying to accept?

body: Purpose: to compare the three exams at a glance. Content: three columns with icons for delivery mode (paper or screen, examiner or microphone), score scales drawn as rulers, and a row of CEFR level markers beneath. Style: neutral; no logos. Board version: a three-column table.

items: Official IELTS, ETS TOEFL and Cambridge English websites (free) for handbooks and sample tests.

blocks.x: Printed handbooks from the school or DIET library and a comparison chart on chart paper.

pts: Major exams undergo extensive psychometric validation — statistical analysis ensuring items function fairly and consistently across large, diverse populations.
This connects directly to Unit 21's test-quality framework, applied at the far more rigorous scale these high-stakes exams demand.
This validation process is a genuine model, in miniature, for the rigour worth aspiring to even in classroom-level assessment.

v: Marked answer sheets from one class test (at least 30 learners); a spreadsheet or squared paper

items: Enter each learner’s score (1 or 0) for each item of a multiple-choice or short-answer section.
Calculate each item’s facility value: the proportion of learners who answered correctly.
Rank learners by total score; take the top third and the bottom third.
For each item, calculate a simple discrimination index: facility in the top group minus facility in the bottom group.
Flag items that are very easy, very hard or that discriminate poorly or negatively, and examine why.
Compare how learners from different schools or language backgrounds performed on each item, a simple first look at fairness.
Support: analyse only ten items.
Challenge: learn how large providers use item response theory and differential item functioning (Bachman and Palmer 2010; Fulcher 2010).

blocks.x: Results for four items from a Class 10 reading test (a fictional class of 45):

lines: Item 3: facility 0.93; discrimination 0.07 → almost everyone got it; tells us little.
Item 7: facility 0.51; discrimination 0.47 → working well.
Item 9: facility 0.38; discrimination –0.13 → stronger readers got it wrong more often; check the key and the wording.
Item 12: facility 0.20; discrimination 0.33 → hard but fair.

blocks.x: Large providers run far more complex analyses on thousands of candidates before items become live, but the logic is the same: check that each item behaves as intended.

body: Purpose: to make facility and discrimination visible. Content: a scatter plot with facility on one axis and discrimination on the other; most items cluster in a shaded ‘healthy’ zone, while a few outliers carry question marks. Style: clean chart with clear labels. Board version: two crossed lines with dots.

items: Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel (free online version) with AVERAGE and simple formulas.
R (free, open source) for teachers who want to go further.

blocks.x: A paper grid with learners as rows and items as columns, tallied by hand.

body: An item with negative discrimination often turns out to have a wrong answer key, or a distractor that is defensibly correct. Checking these items is one of the quickest ways to improve a school test.

pts: Ongoing scholarly debate examines whether these exams genuinely measure real-world communicative competence or a somewhat narrower test-specific construct.
This connects directly to Unit 46's communicative-competence rubric work — do these exams score all four competence dimensions adequately?
This is a genuinely active area of applied linguistics research, not a settled question.

blocks.x: Does the test measure what we teach?

v: Sample tasks from two exams; the four-band rubric of Unit 46

items: Choose one speaking and one writing task from a sample test.
Map each task against the four competences of Unit 27: grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic.
Ask: which real-world situations does this task represent? What does it leave out?
Read the provider’s public band descriptors and note what they reward.
Write a short argument for and against the claim that the task measures real communicative ability.
With C1 learners, discuss how the exam task differs from a real university seminar or job interview.
Support: provide a table with the four competences and the task’s features.
Challenge: read a published critique or validation study and summarize its argument.

lines: A: The speaking test has a real person, so it tests interaction.
B: Partly. But the examiner follows a script, so the candidate rarely has to manage turn-taking or repair the way they would in a real conversation.
A: And there’s no chance to use Hindi or Kannada strategically, even though that’s what bilinguals do in life.
B: That’s a construct choice. The test defines ability as English-only performance.

blocks.x: This debate about what is included in the construct remains open in applied linguistics (Weir 2005; McNamara and Roever 2006).

body: Purpose: to show that a test samples a construct. Content: a large circle labelled ‘communicative ability’ with a smaller circle inside labelled ‘what the task captures’; outside the small circle but inside the large one, labels such as ‘repair’, ‘turn-taking’ and ‘multilingual strategies’. Style: clear Venn-type diagram. Board version: two circles.

items: Official sample tests and public band descriptors (free) from the providers.

pts: These exams' washback effects (Unit 57) are extensively documented, shaping curricula and teaching practice across entire countries and regions.
Some exam providers have actively worked to improve positive washback through task-format changes, informed by this research.
This is one of the clearest, most consequential real-world examples of washback theory in action.

v: Two weeks of your own lesson plans; a coaching-centre timetable or materials (if available)

items: List the activities in two weeks of your exam classes.
Mark each: (a) builds general competence, (b) practises the exam format, (c) teaches test-taking tricks.
Compare with a coaching-centre programme, if you can obtain one.
Discuss: what has the exam changed in what is taught? In how it is taught?
Decide one change to make your preparation more competence-based.
Interview three learners about how they prepare outside class and what they believe the exam rewards.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s tally for two weeks (written for this book):

lines: (a) Competence: 4 lessons (extensive reading, discussion, essay planning).
(b) Format practice: 5 lessons (timed tests, sample tasks).
(c) Tricks: 1 lesson (‘memorize these opening lines for Task 2’).

blocks.x: Decision: Replace the memorized opening lines with a lesson on building an argument from the reader’s point of view. Research on major exams suggests that washback affects content and materials more than teaching methods, and that teachers can shape its direction (Wall 2005; Green 2007).

body: Purpose: to show washback spreading through a system. Content: a stone labelled ‘exam’ dropped into water, with ripples labelled ‘coaching centres’, ‘textbooks’, ‘lessons’ and ‘learners’ beliefs’. Style: simple, evocative. Board version: concentric circles with labels.

items: Google Sheets (free) to tally activity types.

blocks.x: A three-column tally in the teaching journal.

pts: Effective exam preparation, per Unit 66's guidance, builds genuine competence that happens to transfer well to the specific format.
Understanding each exam's specific scoring rubric and task demands supports genuinely targeted, efficient preparation.
Avoid preparation that narrows entirely to test-taking tricks at the expense of the genuine competence the exam aims to certify.

v: A sample writing task and public band descriptors

items: Learners discuss the task topic freely, in English or their home language, to generate ideas.
They read the public band descriptors and, in pairs, restate each criterion in their own words.
The teacher models planning an answer that meets the criteria through genuine argument, not memorized phrases.
Learners write under realistic time limits.
They self-assess against the descriptors, then compare with the teacher’s feedback.
For speaking, record practice answers on phones and self-assess against the speaking descriptors.
Support: provide a planning frame with space for position, reasons, examples and a counter-argument.
Challenge: learners write two versions, one to the time limit and one without, and compare quality.

blocks.x: Learner restatements of public criteria (written for this book, paraphrased):

lines: Task response: answer every part of the question, and make my position clear throughout.
Coherence and cohesion: organize ideas in paragraphs and link them naturally, not with too many ‘moreover’s.
T: What happens if you learn a ready-made introduction by heart?
S1: It saves time.
S2: But the examiner may notice it doesn’t fit the question.
T: Yes, and it doesn’t help you when you actually need to write at university.

body: Purpose: to show preparation built on competence. Content: a tree whose roots are labelled ‘reading, vocabulary, argument, fluency’, whose trunk is ‘real communicative ability’ and whose branches are the exam’s task types. Style: warm illustration. Board version: a simple tree with labels.

items: Official free practice materials from the providers; Google Docs (free) for self-assessment comments.

pts: Score bands correspond to specific, defined proficiency descriptors, not simply an arbitrary ranking — understanding this supports informed institutional decisions.
This connects to Unit 46's can-do-descriptor grounding, applied to interpreting formal, high-stakes exam scores accurately.
Misinterpreting or misusing scores (as a sole, rigid admissions cutoff, for instance) can produce unfair, invalid decisions.

v: Public score descriptors; three fictional score reports

items: Read the public descriptors for two adjacent bands or levels.
For each fictional score report, write what the candidate can probably do, using the descriptors.
Discuss measurement error: why a score is best read as a range rather than a point.
Consider decisions: should a candidate one half-band below a cut-off be rejected automatically?
Draft a short advice note for an institution on responsible score use.
Map the scores to the CEFR using the providers’ published alignment tables, as in Unit 46.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Three fictional profiles with the same overall score:

lines: Candidate A: strong reading and listening, weaker writing.
Candidate B: even profile.
Candidate C: strong speaking, weak reading.
T: A nursing course and a literature course might want different profiles, even with the same overall score.

blocks.x: Every score contains measurement error, so a small difference near a cut-off may not reflect a real difference in ability. Using one score as a rigid, sole criterion risks invalid decisions (AERA, APA and NCME 2014; see Unit 73).

body: Purpose: to show measurement error. Content: a number line with a candidate’s score as a dot and a bracket around it showing a likely range; a vertical cut-off line passes through the bracket. Style: clear. Board version: a line, a dot and brackets.

items: Providers’ score-user guides and CEFR alignment tables (free).

blocks.x: Printed descriptor tables for each band.

pts: Newer, sometimes AI-assisted, testing options continue to emerge, adding both genuine innovation and new evaluation questions to this landscape.
This connects directly to Unit 84's AI-in-ELT discussion and Unit 99's later ethics-of-AI-assessment content.
Staying informed about this evolving landscape supports better learner advising as options genuinely expand.

v: Official information on two newer tests; an evaluation checklist

items: Choose two newer or alternative tests, for example the Duolingo English Test, PTE Academic or Cambridge Linguaskill.
Using official sources, note delivery mode, use of automated or AI scoring, security arrangements and recognition by target institutions.
Apply an evaluation checklist: What evidence of validity is published? Is it independent? Who accepts the score?
Write short, balanced advice for a learner.
Note what you would need to re-check in six months, as policies change quickly.
Learners take a free official sample test and discuss the experience.
Support: provide a completed example for one test.
Challenge: read one published study of automated scoring and summarize its concerns.

lines: This test is cheaper, online and quick to book. However, check that your chosen university accepts it for your course this year, because recognition varies. Its speaking and writing are scored automatically, so practise speaking clearly and completely, but prepare as you would for any exam: by building real skills.

blocks.x: Unit 84 discussed AI in ELT, and Unit 99 returns to the ethics of AI in assessment.

body: Purpose: to guide advice on emerging tests. Content: a signpost with arms labelled ‘Accepted where?’, ‘Evidence?’, ‘Independent?’, ‘Cost?’ and ‘Security?’. Style: simple. Board version: five questions in a list.

items: Official websites of newer tests (free information and sample tests).

blocks.x: A printed checklist kept in the careers corner.

pts: Cost, access, and preparation-resource inequality remain genuine, significant concerns across this major-exam landscape.
This connects directly to Unit 23's inclusive-teaching principles and Unit 73's equity discussion, now grounded in this fuller institutional detail.
Advocating for accessible preparation resources remains a genuine, valuable part of responsible advanced practice.

v: Local information on fees, test centres and free resources

items: In groups, list the costs a learner from your district faces: fees, travel, coaching, devices and data.
Mark which barriers the school or district could reduce.
Collect free, high-quality preparation resources and check their quality.
Plan one action, such as a free after-school preparation club or a shared device schedule.
Link the plan to inclusive-teaching principles (Unit 23) and the ethics discussion of Unit 73.
Invite a former student who has taken the exam to speak about their experience.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An equity map for a rural taluk (written for this book):

lines: Nearest test centre: district headquarters, 70 km. Fee: several thousand rupees; bus travel extra. Coaching: only in the city. Devices: most learners share a family phone.
Action: a weekly free club in the school library using official free materials and one borrowed laptop; senior students mentor juniors in Kannada and English.

blocks.x: Advocating for fair access is part of responsible practice, not an extra.

body: Purpose: to show barriers to access and practical responses. Content: a road to a test centre with obstacles (fee, distance, coaching, device) and small bridges built over each (free club, shared device, mentoring). Style: warm, hopeful. Board version: a line with obstacles and arrows.

items: Official free preparation materials (free) from the providers; Google Classroom (free for schools) for a preparation club.

blocks.x: A library shelf of printed free materials and a peer-mentoring timetable.

body: Take one exam-preparation lesson you teach next week. Before the lesson, label each activity as competence, format or trick. Replace one trick with a competence-building activity, and ask learners afterwards which part helped them most.

dek: Unit 92 of 100: the institutions, psychometrics, and systemic effects behind the world's major English exams — examined in the depth Tier III's introduction (Unit 66) began.

aims.x: Unit 66 prepared C1 learners for high-stakes exams, and Unit 73 examined the ethics and validity of such testing. This unit looks behind the counter at the institutions themselves: how the major international English exams are built, validated and used, what they can and cannot tell us, and how teachers can advise learners well. Many Indian learners, and many of their parents, invest heavily in these exams. Teachers who understand them can prepare learners efficiently and protect them from poor advice.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: compare the purposes, formats and score scales of IELTS, TOEFL iBT and the Cambridge English Qualifications;
explain in plain terms how psychometric validation works, and apply simple item analysis to a classroom test;
evaluate construct-validity arguments about what these exams measure;
describe documented washback from major exams and its implications for local teaching;
plan exam preparation that builds competence while respecting task demands;
interpret scores, bands and measurement error responsibly;
advise learners on newer testing options, including AI-scored tests, with appropriate caution;
identify equity barriers and practical ways to reduce them.

why: Why this matters. These exams shape millions of learners' academic and professional pathways. Understanding their actual design and limitations supports better-informed teaching and advising.

background.x: Large-scale tests are held to professional standards that set out how evidence for validity, reliability and fairness should be gathered (AERA, APA and NCME 2014). Modern validity theory, developed especially by Samuel Messick (1989), treats validity not as a property of a test but as the degree to which evidence supports the interpretations and uses of its scores. Lyle Bachman and Adrian Palmer (2010) turned this into an ‘assessment use argument’: a chain of claims from a test-taker’s performance to a decision, each of which must be supported. Unit 21 introduced validity, reliability and practicality at classroom level; this unit applies the same ideas at the scale of millions of candidates.

The major exam providers publish research on their tests, and independent scholars study them too. Researchers have examined whether these exams capture real academic or professional communication (Weir 2005; Fulcher 2010), and how they shape teaching. Studies such as Dianne Wall’s (2005) in Sri Lanka and Anthony Green’s (2007) on IELTS preparation showed that washback is real but complex: exams change what is taught more readily than how it is taught, and effects depend on teachers, materials and institutions (Alderson and Wall 1993; see Unit 57).

Tests also have social consequences. Elana Shohamy (2001) described the power of tests to act as gatekeepers, and Tim McNamara and Carsten Roever (2006) examined their role in migration and citizenship. In India, IELTS and similar exams stand between many young people and study or work abroad, and families may spend large sums on fees and coaching. NEP 2020 calls for assessment that tests core competencies and reduces the need for coaching (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). For English teachers, the professional task is to help learners meet real gatekeeping demands without letting a test’s format narrow the language they learn.

items: Comparison chart. An accurate, sourced comparison of three major exams, with the date of checking.
Item analysis. Facility and discrimination values for one classroom test, with decisions on weak items.
Washback audit. A tally of two weeks’ preparation lessons and one change towards competence-building.
Advice note. Balanced written advice for a learner choosing a test, or for an institution using scores.
How much of your exam preparation builds competence, and how much only practises format?
Which of your own tests has never been checked item by item?
What would you say to a parent who believes one exam is ‘the best’ for every purpose?
How do you explain measurement error to learners anxious about a half band?
Which of your learners are most disadvantaged by cost and distance, and what could your school do?
How do you check whether your information about exams is still current?

Fulcher, G. 2010. Practical Language Testing. London: Hodder Education.

terms.def: A framework in which test developers must justify each link from a test performance to the interpretation of scores, the decisions made and their consequences for test takers (Bachman and Palmer 2010).
The use of software to assign scores to spoken or written performances; it raises questions of validity, fairness and transparency, especially when the scores inform important decisions.
The extent to which a test measures the construct it claims to measure, and not other abilities; for example, whether a writing score reflects writing rather than typing speed.

The score on a test that divides one level or decision from another, such as pass and fail; setting it requires careful judgement because small differences in score can lead to very different decisions.

In item analysis, a measure of how well a test item separates stronger from weaker learners, calculated simply as the facility value in the top-scoring group minus the facility value in the bottom-scoring group.
In item analysis, the proportion of test-takers who answer an item correctly, from 0 to 1. A value of 0.93 means almost everyone got it right, so the item tells the teacher little.
The statistical and theoretical process of gathering evidence that a test measures what it claims to measure consistently and fairly.
A statistical estimate of how far an observed test score is likely to differ from a learner’s ‘true’ score because of measurement error. It reminds users that a score is a band, not an exact point.
The principle that a test gives all test takers an equal opportunity to show their ability, through unbiased content, appropriate accommodations, consistent administration and just use of scores.

The effect of a test on teaching and learning, which may be positive or negative (Alderson and Wall 1993). Board examinations that test only reading and writing often lead to neglect of listening and speaking.
